cards.prompt: Load a CSV file at csv_path into a DataFrame.
cards.why: read_csv() is pandas' default entry point for tabular text files — it infers a header row, column dtypes, and a default integer index automatically.
cards.whenToUse: Loading data that lives in a plain .csv file, which is most real-world tabular data.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting read_csv() returns a new DataFrame — you need to assign the result to a variable to keep it.
cards.example:
#    order_date region category  revenue  units
# 0  2024-01-05   West    Shoes      120     12

cards.prompt: Load csv_path and preview just its first 3 rows in one line.
cards.why: Chaining .head() right after read_csv() is a fast way to sanity-check a load without printing the whole file.
cards.whenToUse: The very first thing to run against unfamiliar data, before trusting anything else about it.
cards.commonMistake: Loading the full file first (into a named variable) when only a peek is needed — chaining is fine for a one-off check.
cards.example:
#    order_date region category  revenue  units
# 0  2024-01-05   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1  2024-01-06   East    Shoes       95      9
# 2  2024-01-07   West     Bags       80      8

cards.prompt: Load csv_path using the order_date column as the row index instead of a default integer index.
cards.why: index_col tells read_csv which column to promote to the index during the load, instead of doing set_index() as a separate step afterward.
cards.whenToUse: The file has an obvious natural key (a date, an id) that you'll repeatedly look up by.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming index_col parses the column as a date automatically — without parse_dates too, it stays plain text.
cards.example:
#             region category  revenue  units
# order_date
# 2024-01-05    West    Shoes      120     12

cards.prompt: Load only the region and revenue columns from csv_path, skipping the rest.
cards.why: usecols skips parsing the other columns entirely, which is both faster and avoids loading data you don't need.
cards.whenToUse: A wide file where you only care about a handful of columns.
cards.commonMistake: Loading everything with read_csv() and then dropping columns afterward — usecols is more efficient since it skips parsing them at all.

cards.prompt: Load csv_path, forcing the revenue column to load as float instead of pandas' inferred type.
cards.why: dtype takes a dict mapping column name to the type it should load as, overriding pandas' automatic inference for just that column.
cards.whenToUse: The inferred type is wrong or inconvenient — e.g. an id column read as int that you need as text, or a number you want as float from the start.
cards.commonMistake: Trying to fix a wrong dtype after loading instead of specifying it up front — both work, but dtype= avoids a wasted intermediate representation.
cards.example: # revenue column loads as 120.0, 95.0, ... (float64) instead of int64

cards.prompt: Load csv_path, parsing order_date as an actual datetime column instead of plain text.
cards.why: parse_dates converts the listed columns to datetime64 during the load, so date arithmetic and .dt accessors work right away.
cards.whenToUse: Any CSV column that represents a date or timestamp — text dates can't be compared or sorted chronologically without this.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting to parse dates, then being confused when df['order_date'] > '2024-01-01' compares strings instead of actual dates.
cards.example: # order_date column dtype becomes datetime64[ns] instead of object

cards.prompt: Load only the first 3 data rows of csv_path, without reading the rest of the file at all.
cards.why: nrows stops reading after n rows during parsing — unlike head(), it never reads the rest of the file in the first place.
cards.whenToUse: A huge file where you just need a quick preview and don't want to wait for (or hold in memory) the full load.
cards.commonMistake: Using pd.read_csv(csv_path).head(3) on a huge file — that still reads and parses every row before trimming to 3.
cards.example: # same 3 rows as head(3), but the file was never fully read

cards.prompt: Load csv_path while skipping its very first line, before pandas even looks for a header.
cards.why: skiprows removes lines from the file before header inference happens — skipping the real header row means the first data row gets mistaken for the header instead.
cards.whenToUse: Files with junk lines (a title, a comment) before the real header — skip exactly those lines, not the header itself.
cards.commonMistake: Using skiprows=1 on a normal file expecting it to 'skip the header' — it skips whatever line is first, which usually is the header, leaving the first data row misread as column names.
cards.example: # columns become '2024-01-05', 'West', 'Shoes', '120', '12' — the real header is gone

cards.prompt: Load csv_path_no_header (a file with no header row at all) and supply column names yourself.
cards.why: header=None tells pandas the first line is data, not labels; names= then supplies the column labels pandas would otherwise have inferred.
cards.whenToUse: Raw data exports that start directly with data, no header line.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting header=None — without it, pandas treats the first data row as column names, silently losing a row.
cards.example:
#    order_date region category  revenue  units
# 0  2024-01-05   West    Shoes      120     12

cards.prompt: Load csv_path_missing, treating the literal string '?' as a missing value.
cards.why: Real-world CSVs mark missing data with all sorts of placeholders ('?', 'N/A', '-') — na_values tells pandas which strings to treat as NaN instead of literal text.
cards.whenToUse: A source file uses a non-standard placeholder for missing data that pandas wouldn't recognize by default.
cards.commonMistake: Skipping na_values and getting a column silently loaded as text (object) because a placeholder like '?' prevented it from being read as numeric.
cards.example: # the '?' revenue cell becomes NaN, and the column loads as float64

cards.prompt: After loading csv_path_missing with '?' treated as missing, count how many missing values landed in each column.
cards.why: Chaining isna().sum() right after a load is a fast way to confirm which columns actually have gaps, and how many.
cards.whenToUse: Right after loading any new CSV, before deciding whether to dropna() or fillna().
cards.commonMistake: Running isna().sum() before specifying na_values — without it, placeholders like '?' are just text and won't be flagged as missing.
cards.example:
# order_date    0
# region        0
# category      0
# revenue       1
# units         1
# dtype: int64

cards.prompt: Convert df into CSV text (as a string), without writing to a file, and without including the index column.
cards.why: to_csv() with no path argument returns the CSV content as a string instead of writing a file — handy for previewing exactly what would be saved.
cards.whenToUse: Checking what a file would contain before writing it, or handing CSV text to code that expects a string, not a file.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting index=False — by default to_csv() writes the row index as its own leading column, which is rarely wanted for a clean export.

cards.prompt: Right after loading csv_path, check every column's inferred dtype in one call. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: Checking dtypes immediately after a load confirms pandas inferred what you expected — especially for numbers and dates.
cards.whenToUse: Right after any read_csv() call, before trusting a column's type.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming a column that looks numeric loaded as numeric — any stray non-numeric value in the column forces it to load as object (text).
cards.example:
# order_date    object
# region        object
# category      object
# revenue        int64
# units          int64
# dtype: object

cards.prompt: Which loads csv_path with order_date as a real datetime index (not just a text column)?
cards.why: index_col alone promotes the column to the index but leaves it as text; parse_dates=True (combined with index_col) tells pandas to also parse that index column as dates.
cards.whenToUse: Time-series-style data where you'll do date-based slicing (like df.loc['2024-01']) and need a real DatetimeIndex, not text labels.
cards.commonMistake: Setting index_col='order_date' without parse_dates and expecting date-based slicing to work — it silently stays as string labels.
